title: The Journalists Who Left Russia—But Can’t Escape It
gist: Review of Julia Loktev's six-hour documentary 'My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile', following journalists from Russia's last independent TV channel Dozhd into exile after 2022; it documents Kremlin repression reaching abroad (threats, suspected poisoning, in-absentia sentences) and Dozhd's continued reach of 13 million viewers via VPNs, while the exiles wrestle with collective responsibility for Russia's war.

insights.claim: After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, new censorship laws made independent journalism punishable by up to 15 years in prison, prompting Dozhd (TV Rain) journalists to flee within days to Istanbul, Tbilisi, Prague, and Tel Aviv.
insights.speaker: Anastasia Edel
insights.so_what: Illustrates the near-total closure of Russia's domestic information space.
insights.quote: punishable by up to 15 years in prison

insights.claim: Russian courts continue to punish dissent harshly: journalist Ivan Safronov received 22 years on fabricated treason charges, artist Sasha Skochilenko got seven years for anti-war price tags, and anchor Valeria Ratnikova was sentenced in absentia to seven and a half years.
insights.speaker: Anastasia Edel
insights.so_what: Signals entrenched authoritarianism and low odds of domestic political liberalization in Russia.
insights.quote: in Russia, the price of truth is your freedom

insights.claim: Kremlin pressure follows exiles abroad: IStories journalists in Prague received anonymous threats citing passport numbers and flight reservations, a supposed human rights lawyer had worked for Moscow police, and Novaya Gazeta's Elena Kostyuchenko believes she was poisoned in Munich in October 2022.
insights.speaker: Anastasia Edel
insights.so_what: Transnational repression is a persistent security risk in European host countries.
insights.locator: The hope of finding safety outside Russia

insights.claim: Dozhd's coverage presented opposition leader Alexey Navalny's 2024 death in prison as a killing, saying openly what many in Russia were afraid to say.
insights.speaker: Anastasia Edel
insights.so_what: Context for the elimination of organized opposition inside Russia.
insights.locator: Or your life. A sizable part

insights.claim: Dozhd, now operating from the Netherlands, still reached 13 million viewers as of 2023 by its own count, mostly via VPNs and proxies, after on-air missteps cost it its Latvian broadcasting license.
insights.speaker: Anastasia Edel
insights.so_what: A sizable Russian audience still seeks non-Kremlin information, sustaining VPN demand despite censorship.
insights.quote: still reaches 13 million as of 2023, according to Dozhd
insights.locator: From its new home in the Netherlands

insights.claim: Exiled journalists like Ksenia Mironova and Anna Nemzer are archiving two decades of independent Russian journalism to preserve it against Kremlin attempts to erase it.
insights.speaker: Anastasia Edel
insights.so_what: Low direct investment relevance; signals long-horizon information-war dynamics.
insights.locator: Ksyusha is neither a victim nor a tragic heroine

themes.theme: Collective responsibility and social attitudes in Russia

insights.claim: Exiled Russian journalists face constant demands to answer for their country's war from Georgian and Latvian hosts and Ukrainian sources, while their own parents urge them to come home, reflecting deep societal division.
insights.speaker: Anastasia Edel
insights.so_what: Generational and diaspora splits underline weak domestic pressure on the Kremlin to end the war.
insights.quote: You feel like it’s 1941 and you’re simultaneously the German and the Jew

insights.claim: Kostyuchenko argues Russia's liberal journalists documented the coming of fascism in detail but failed to stop it because 'we didn't want to sacrifice our comfort.'
insights.speaker: Anastasia Edel
insights.so_what: Self-critique suggests elite opposition lacked the will to constrain the regime—little near-term regime-change prospect.
insights.quote: We didn’t want to sacrifice our comfort.
insights.locator: Perhaps no one takes up these questions

insights.claim: A journalist's father insisted the war is in Ukraine, not Russia, illustrating how many Russians remain insulated from and indifferent to the war—the author calls them the 'perpetually silent majority'.
insights.speaker: Anastasia Edel
insights.so_what: Public indifference reduces domestic political costs for the Kremlin of continuing the war.
insights.locator: The hope of finding safety outside Russia
